title: The Parenting Trap
author: Jonathan Rothwell
summary: Rothwell, Gallup's Principal Economist and a father of four, argues that decades of permissive parenting created a governance vacuum that made Gen Z uniquely vulnerable to a screen-based childhood and its mental-health consequences. Using the Maccoby-Martin warmth-vs-demandingness framework and Baumrind's authoritative-parenting lineage, he shows that recent Gallup survey data find no meaningful generational change in parental warmth but a large decline in demandingness, specifically in punishment for wrongdoing and enforced rules. External data line up with that story: the GSS "obey" rating fell from 40% in 1986 to 18% in 2024, and teen summer employment dropped from 57% in 1976 to 38% in 2024. The screen-time data show that fewer than half of parents of children three and older set screen limits, and only 30% of parents of adolescents do, yet the teens of parents who do limit screens spend roughly 1.4 fewer hours per day on social media and have meaningfully better mental health outcomes. His prescription is to respect parental authority: set clear rules, enforce them, default to "no social media" and toward less distracting communication devices like smartwatches, and treat children's long-term wellbeing as worth short-term displeasure.
points: The Gallup 2024 retrospective survey finds generational warmth roughly unchanged (44% of 1930-49 cohort vs 41% of 1995-2006 cohort agreed their father was "very warm and affectionate"), but demandingness items (rule enforcement, punishment) declined significantly.

External corroboration: percentage of US parents listing "to obey" as one of the two most important things for children to learn fell from 40% (1986) to 18% (2024) on the General Social Survey; teen summer employment fell from 57% (1976) to 38% (2024).
US teens report roughly five hours per day on social media (2023 Gallup), yet fewer than half of parents of children 3+ restrict screen time, and only 30% of parents of adolescents do.

Teens of parents who restrict screens report about 1.4 fewer hours per day on social media and shift that time to homework/chores/hobbies/sports; among parents high in demandingness AND restricting screens, 14% reported their child had been at least sometimes depressed vs 38% among permissive + unrestricted parents, and 20% vs 50% spent 5+ hours/day on social media.
His default recommendation: no social media, smartwatches or basic phones over smartphones where possible, clear and enforced rules, children's long-term wellbeing over short-term pleasing.
quotes: While it is well documented that social media poses significant risks to youth mental health, the long-term cultural trends that inflated its influence have received much less attention. I argue that a decades-long shift to permissive parenting created a governance vacuum, an absence of necessary rules and expectations, that left Gen Z uniquely vulnerable, providing the ideal environment for a screen-based childhood to take hold and compound the prevailing mental health challenges of adolescents.

We found little to no difference in parents' warmth, affection, or responsiveness. For example, 44% of adults born between 1930 and 1949 agreed with the statement their father "was very warm and affectionate toward you." For those born between 1995 and 2006, 41% agreed. There were, however, much larger differences in the demanding aspects of parenting.

The measured fall in demanding parenting comes at a time when adolescents are confronted with new technological temptations that require parental guidance. Thus, the partial relinquishing of parental governance increases vulnerability to the harms of social media, video games, and other habit-forming products.

Consistent with the broader argument, parents who do restrict screen time tend to have children who report less time using social media. On average, teens whose parents set limits report about 1.4 fewer hours per day on social media. They also report less time spent on video games, less time alone, and more time devoted to homework, chores, hobbies, and practicing sports or arts, patterns that are generally associated with better mental health outcomes.

Ultimately, even without the cooperation of tech companies, decisions about whether and how a child uses digital technology belong to parents. Pleasing children in the short term is not as important as ensuring their long-term well-being.” Archived from After Babel (guest post) on April 21, 2026 by Tim.
